question.problem: Find a point that satisfies the mean value theorem for $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+y$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨1,3⟩,$ respectively.
question.worked_solution:
The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+y$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨1,3⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,3)-f(0,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨1,3⟩-⟨0,1⟩) \\ ({1}^{2}+3)-({0}^{2}+1) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,2⟩ \\ 3 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨2x,1⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨2{c}_{1},1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨1,2⟩ \\ 3 & =⟨2{c}_{1},1⟩\cdot ⟨1,2⟩ \\ 3 & =2{c}_{1}+2 \\ 1 & =2{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-1}{3-1} & =\frac{x-0}{1-0} \\ \frac{y-1}{2} & =x \\ y & =2x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & =2{c}_{1}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking into account that ${c}_{1}=\frac{1}{2},$ we obtain that ${c}_{2}=2\cdot \frac{1}{2}+1=2.$ So, the point $C$ that satisfies the mean value theorem is $(\frac{1}{2},2).$
